blocks.en: In Taiwan, 99.2% of farms are small-scale (under 2 hectares), together managing 85.3% of the island's agricultural land, yet many of these farmers face growing climate challenges with limited resources to respond. Through geospatial analysis, we mapped climate patterns, farmland distribution, and socioeconomic conditions to understand where these challenges are most severe. We also connected our findings with farmer interviews and field visits to better understand the people behind the data. By identifying communities where climate risks and limited resources overlap, our analysis helps us understand where ReLEAF could make the greatest difference, bringing plant protection closer to the farmers who need it most.

blocks.en: Single interviews cannot establish whether what one farmer describes is an isolated hardship or a structural pattern. Answering this requires working at a different scale entirely: parcel-level land records, station-level climate data, and demographic surveys, aggregated across all counties rather than gathered farm by farm. This is where the role of geospatial analysis comes in, complementary to case studies.

blocks.en: Existing geospatial studies of Taiwanese agriculture tend to treat variables in isolation: climate-trend analyses map warming or rainfall change without reference to who farms the affected land, while agricultural demographic surveys report vulnerability without a spatial climate layer to test it against. None, to our knowledge, overlay farmland fragmentation, climate volatility, and a documented crop-stress yield effect at the parcel or township level simultaneously. This page presents our method and findings.

blocks.en: Rice is the primary calorie source for more than half the world's population (FAO, 2004), and across Asia it is grown at every scale — from smallholder plots to industrial acreage — as both a staple food and an economic backbone. The most dangerous part of this dependency is not the stress a farmer can see coming; it is the stress that arrives when no one is in the field to see it—during night time.
blocks.text: Rice is the primary calorie source for more than half the world's population (FAO, 2004), and across Asia it is grown at every scale — from smallholder plots to industrial acreage — as both a staple food and an economic backbone. The most dangerous part of this dependency is not the stress a farmer can see coming; it is the stress that arrives when no one is in the field to see it—during night time.

blocks.en: Farming has always been a practice of response: a farmer notices wilting, discoloration, or dry soil, and intervenes. That model assumes stress leaves a visible trace in time to act on. Rising nighttime temperatures break that assumption. A 25-year record from the International Rice Research Institute’s farm in the Philippines (Peng et al., 2004) showed that from 1979 to 2003, nighttime minimum temperatures rose roughly three times faster than daytime maximums, and that dry-season grain yield fell by about 10% for every 1°C rise in nighttime temperature, while daytime heat alone had no significant effect. The leading explanation is that warm nights keep the plant’s metabolism running in the dark, burning through the sugars it stored during the day before they can be committed to grain.

blocks.en: What matters most here is not the size of that loss but its timing. The damage happens overnight, leaves the canopy looking entirely healthy by sunrise, and only becomes visible weeks later as a lighter harvest. A run of warm nights during grain filling can cost a season’s yield one year and miss the critical window entirely the next, so there is no reliable signal to watch for and no point at which a farmer could have stepped in. Even an attentive, experienced farmer cannot respond to stress that happens on the plant’s schedule rather than their own. As warming makes these events more frequent and less predictable, protection that waits for symptoms will increasingly arrive too late.

blocks.en: The underlying fragmentation innate to Taiwan is now colliding with a warming rate that continues to outpace tradition’s ability to adapt. For nearly a century, Taiwan’s average temperature crept upward by around 0.11ºC per decade – slow enough that a farmer could spend a lifetime farming and barely notice. Since 1991, that rate has nearly tripled to 0.29ºC per decade, with 2024 becoming Taiwan’s hottest year on record, with Taipei logging 63 days above 35ºC. blocks.en: When asked how she prepares for the dry season, Ms. Chen described layering dried weeds across her soil so morning dew soaked slowly into the ground, carrying her plants up to three weeks between checks. It is a schedule calibrated over decades on one plot of land, and it assumes stress will build at the pace it always has. Contrary to the certainty, a 2022 global study led by Hong Kong Polytechnic University found roughly 34-46% of flash droughts reached drought conditions within five days, with that share rising over 2000–2020 while frequency mostly held steady. Farmers’ knowledge hasn’t changed, but the window it was built for has shrunk. Closing that gap means protection already in place before stress arrives.

blocks.en: Taiwan, at just 36 200 square kilometers, consumes more than 300 kilograms of fertilizer per hectare – compared to roughly 128 kilograms per hectare in the United States, a country 9.83 million square kilometers in size (Refer to Figure 6 and Figure 7). Part of this gap comes down to spatial pressure: only about a quarter of Taiwan’s land is viable for agriculture, versus roughly two-fifths in the US. But fertilizer use scaled to compensate for land scarcity comes at a cost. While fertilizer has propped up yields, excessive application strains underground soil biology and degrades soil quality over time.

blocks.en: That centralization problem isn't just chemical — it's logistical. To quantify it, we built a nationwide GIS routing model connecting every one of Taiwan's 613 registered fertilizer companies to real farmland (Refer to Figure 8): 2 792 536 individual parcels, aggregated by township into 346 demand nodes covering roughly 743 500 hectares of arable land. Each company is routed only to farmland inside its own county, using road-network distance rather than straight-line distance — the model won't let a company shortcut to a closer field across a county line, because that's not how actual distribution works.

blocks.en: Even under this best-case, same-county assumption, the model shows that centralized fertilizer production still has to travel: every kilogram makes a real trip along real roads before it reaches a real field, adding cost for time and emissions that a farm averaging under 1.1 hectares absorbs disproportionately relative to its output. A production model that instead manufactures the protectant on-site — at the scale of a single farm or a shared township reactor — removes that shipping step entirely.

blocks.en: In consideration to confirming and quantitatively measuring on-site on-demand deployment in fields, a highly important factor to consider is how well our engineered bacteria responds to light, how quickly is the response, and how much protectant is ultimately produced. The light plate apparatus (LPA) allows for quantitative analysis and accurate measurement rather than blindly answering these concerns qualitatively.
blocks.text: In consideration to confirming and quantitatively measuring on-site on-demand deployment in fields, a highly important factor to consider is how well our engineered bacteria responds to light, how quickly is the response, and how much protectant is ultimately produced. The light plate apparatus (LPA) allows for quantitative analysis and accurate measurement rather than blindly answering these concerns qualitatively.

blocks.en: The LPA is a 24-tube LED array that holds engineered Bacillus subtilis WB800 (CcaS/CcaR system) under six defined light conditions at once: green light (~535 nm) induces protectant production, and red light (~670 nm) halts it. Each condition is one column of four resistance-matched LEDs lighting four tubes. Intensity is set by Arduino PWM through three MOSFETs, one per tier (low, mid, high), and held constant for the whole run. Rather than a single endpoint reading, we sample each condition over time and track protectant output across the full period.

blocks.en: Chlorophyll content as a physiological readout
blocks.text: Chlorophyll content as a physiological readout

blocks.en: Chlorophyll degradation is one of the earliest and most reliable indicators of salt stress in plants. Sodium accumulation disrupts chloroplast structure, accelerates chlorophyll breakdown, and suppresses photosynthetic capacity well before visible wilting occurs. Thus, chlorophyll content serves as a quantitative proxy for stress damage, and by extension, for protectant efficacy. A plant that retains more chlorophyll under identical salt exposure is a plant that is better protected.

blocks.en: The Nantou farmer’s response to any proposed treatment was specific and immediate: a natural protectant would be acceptable, provided its compatibility with organic certification requirements could be confirmed. This farm is in the process of transitioning to certified organic status, and any input under consideration must remain compatible with that transition. This has direct implications for product positioning: a biological, GMO-derived treatment from our engineered bacteria such as ACC-deaminase is not merely acceptable to this segment of farmers but may represent the only category of input such farmers are willing to consider. This also identifies a concrete requirement for market entry, as confirming compatibility with organic certification standards is not a clean line, rather a gray area, making farmers in their trial stage of the organic transition unwilling to risk it and try out the product.

blocks.en: As previously mentioned, Raster data and vector data are the most common and fundamental data types utilized within QGIS, one covering pixels, and the other utilizing lines/ points. Raster data sets are discrete and continuous cells (pixels) that represent data that gradually varies across space, also classifying them into different categories. Oftentimes, Raster data is used to present temperature or elevation maps as they can be visualized as continuous and gradient-like. Conversely, Vector data are scalable values that only depict discrete features like data points or lines; they are most commonly used to establish borders or outlines of files.

blocks.en: When researching global geospatial data, running into data sets with hundreds to thousands of numerics is inevitable. Oftentimes, these data sets are unorganized and condensed with tons of information, and they come in formats QGIS does not support, with field types that are inconsistent from row to row, no geometry column, or a non-standard text encoding, so QGIS cannot read them directly. Moreover with varying coordinate systems, data from different sources may have varying coordinates, unaligning in the software. Manually reconstructing thousands of numerics is time-consuming and could contain operator error, especially for students unfamiliar or non-professionals of the GIS field.

blocks.en: To address the following, we developed a broad, reusable prompt that generates data files in formats that QGIS is able to properly analyze (GeoJSON, CSV, SHP) from arbitrary raw input data. The following prompt, rather than being hard-wired to only analyze data sets beneficial to our project (Taiwan Farmland and Climate Volatility), the prompt is generalized so that any team desirable of use Geospatial Analyses can adapt it to develop their own geographic data set.

blocks.en: We designed the following prompt as a contribution other future iGEM teams can utilize and incorporate into their own project. As aforementioned, when integrating spatial analysis into desired projects, regardless of the specific data sets, it is bound to run into similar data overload problems, utilizing this prompt allows for easier data organization experiences.

blocks.en: Our prompt, presented in Text 1, demonstrates that rules are grounded in established prompt engineering research rather than built ad hoc. Restricting the model to only use provided data reflects grounding research, shown to reduce hallucination (Addlesee, 2024). Flagging missing, ambiguous, or unusable values instead of guessing reflects calibration and abstention research, addressing a known tendency of LLMs to answer confidently rather than admit uncertainty. Requiring transparent calculation logic follows chain-of-thought prompting, shown to improve accuracy on multi-step tasks (Wei et al., 2022). Detecting and stating the coordinate reference system before use follows self-verification prompting, where an assumption is externalized so it can be checked rather than embedded silently in the output. Finally, requiring the output to exactly match the requested format (CSV, SHP, or GeoJSON) reflects structured output practices common to established frameworks such as CO-STAR and RTF, which produce more consistent, usable results than open-ended formatting instructions.
